title: Hypoxic Load and Average Oxygen‐Saturation During Sleep and Wake Are Associated With Cognitive Function in Obstructive Sleep Apnea

sections.abstract:
Cognitive processes commonly affected by obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) are more strongly associated with hypoxic load parameters than the apnea‐hypopnea index (AHI). Additionally, lower SpO 2 during wake affects cognition, emphasising the need for concurrent assessment with sleep SpO 2 . This study examined which OSA severity parameters best predict cognitive performance and the role of wake SpO 2 . Sixty‐one participants (53% female), with an average age of 46.9 years (range 19–79), completed a three‐night self‐applied polysomnography (PSG) and a digital neurocognitive battery. Oxygen saturation‐based PSG parameters predicted immediate recall, vigilance, and processing speed, whereas the AHI did not. Greater hypoxic severity from 100% SpO 2 baseline was the strongest predictor of slower processing speed ( χ 2 (6) = 17.74, p = 0.007) ( β = −5.72, p = 0.023). Lower average SpO 2 during sleep most strongly predicted immediate recall ( χ 2 (6) = 28.94, p < 0.001) ( β = 0.38, p = 0.03) and vigilance ( χ 2 (6) = 16.72, p = 0.010) ( β = 0.15, p = 0.002). Additionally, lower wake SpO 2 was associated with reduced vigilance performance. The results confirm the AHI's limitation in capturing OSA symptom severity and highlight the stronger associations between oxygen saturation‐based OSA parameters and cognitive abilities. Furthermore, we recommend incorporating wake SpO 2 measures in sleep research to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between SpO 2 and cognitive abilities.

Keywords: apnea‐hypopnea index, cognitive flexibility, obstructive sleep apnea, oxygen saturation, verbal memory, vigilance, visuospatial abilities
sections.introduction:
Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is characterised by repeated upper airway obstruction and increased respiratory effort during sleep (Bassetti et al. 2021 ). OSA severity is typically assessed using the apnea‐hypopnea index (AHI), which counts the number of respiratory events per hour of sleep, measured by polysomnography (PSG) or home sleep apnea testing (HSAT) (American Academy of Sleep Medicine 2014 ). Based on the AHI, < 5 events per hour is considered as no OSA, 5–14.9 mild OSA, 15.0–29.9 moderate OSA, and ≥ 30 severe OSA (AASM 1999 ). However, the AHI has been criticised for overlooking the severity of these respiratory events by not considering their length and/or severity. Hypoxic load parameters, which capture desaturation depth and duration, have been considered as potentially better indicators of OSA severity (Kulkas, Tiihonen, Eskola, et al. 2013 ; Martinez‐Garcia et al. 2023 ; Mazzotti et al. 2018 ). They have also been associated with commonly seen cognitive difficulties in OSA, whereas the AHI has not (Batool‐Anwar et al. 2014 ; Blackwell et al. 2015 ; Hrubos‐Strøm et al. 2012 ; Kainulainen et al. 2020 ; Quan et al. 2011 ; Vakulin et al. 2016 ). These difficulties are in attention and vigilance, verbal memory, executive function, and information processing speed (Andreou et al. 2014 ; Bucks et al. 2017 ; Engleman and Joffe 1999 ; Kainulainen et al. 2020 ; Seda et al. 2021 ; Vanek et al. 2020 ). Kainulainen et al. ( 2020 ) found severe desaturations to be the strongest PSG‐related indicators of poor vigilance performance in OSA, which had no correlation with the AHI. Vigilance has also been associated with hypoxia time (SpO 2 duration < 90%) (Alomri et al. 2021 ) and verbal memory with average SpO 2 during sleep and not the AHI (Hrubos‐Strøm et al. 2012 ; Thorisdottir et al. 2024 ).

Independent of sleep research, cognitive performance is influenced by blood oxygen supply during wakefulness. A study among 112 adults, not suffering from sleep disordered breathing, found that those with low awake cerebral oxygen saturation (43%–49.9%) performed worse on neurocognitive tests measuring delayed memory and processing speed compared to those with normal values (60.0%–79.9%) (Carlson et al. 2011 ). Studies have also shown positive effects of highly concentrated oxygen supply during wakefulness on cognitive performance among young adults and the elderly (Kim et al. 2013 ; Moss et al. 1998 ). This drew our attention to a gap in sleep research, where the relationship between cognitive performance and OSA severity has been explored using both traditional OSA and hypoxic load measures during sleep, overlooking the potential effect of SpO 2 levels during wake.

The main objective of this study was to examine which OSA severity parameters most strongly predicted cognitive abilities, including traditional parameters such as the AHI and novel hypoxic load parameters. The second aim was to study the correlation between cognitive performance and average SpO 2 during sleep vs. wake. Five neurocognitive tests were used measuring verbal memory, vigilance, processing speed, cognitive flexibility, and visuospatial abilities. We hypothesised that hypoxic load parameters would better predict cognitive function compared to the AHI, and that average SpO 2 during wake would be associated with cognitive function independently of OSA severity.
sections.methods:
A total of 61 participants (mean age 46.9 years, range 19–79 years, 53% females) participated in the current study, which was a part of a larger pilot study in the Sleep Revolution project (Arnardottir et al. 2022 ). A total of 80 individuals from the general population were initially recruited for participation. Sixteen individuals withdrew participation before the study started and three during the study. All 61 participants completed an in‐laboratory digital neurocognitive battery followed by a three‐night self‐applied PSG (Dimitri et al. 2024 ).

All cognitive assessments were completed on a computer at Reykjavik University. The tasks were administered online using the Inquisit platform (Millisecond 2021 ).

A modified version of the original Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test was administered to measure verbal memory (Schmidt 1996 ). The original version consists of 15 nouns that are read aloud five times (A1–A5) to the participant who then immediately retrieves as many words as possible after each trial. In this version, the words were pre‐recorded by a native speaker of Icelandic and played through headphones, and instead of the participants retrieving the words aloud, they typed the words into a textbox on the computer. Thereafter, two other cognitive tests were administered that took 15–20 min; both were non‐verbal. Then, the delayed recall of list A (A6) was performed. Since the delay varied slightly between participants, it was not used in the analysis. Immediate recall (A1), total recall (A1 + A2 + A3 + A4 + A5) and learning over trials (LOT) ((total recall)—(Trial A1) × 5) were included in the analysis, with higher scores indicating better performance.

The TOL is a spatial problem‐solving task measuring executive function, more specifically cognitive flexibility (Schnirman et al. 1998 ). With a computer mouse, participants were instructed to move three coloured disks onto three poles of different sizes, from an initial state to a goal state, in as few moves as possible. The poles could hold one, two, or three disks. Two patterns were presented; on the left side of the screen was a starting pattern, and on the right was the goal pattern. Only one disk could be moved at a time. Participants first solved a test pattern, followed by 12 patterns that were included in the total score. For each problem, 3 points were granted if the correct solution was found on the first attempt, 2 points if found on the second attempt, 1 point if three attempts were needed, and 0 points if the third attempt failed. The overall score was the sum of scores for the 12 problems (0–36) where a higher score indicated better performance.

The PVT was administered to measure vigilance, the ability to maintain alertness for a certain period of time and readiness to respond to stimulus changes that occur infrequently over a prolonged period of time (Strauss et al. 2006 ). Participants were instructed to press the spacebar on a keyboard to respond to a target (red stopwatch) that appeared in the middle of the computer screen. The red stopwatch was displayed randomly at intervals of 2–10 s. Participants were required to respond as fast as possible by pressing the spacebar when the target was displayed. The computer showed their reaction time (RT), or an error message if they gave an invalid response by pressing the spacebar before the target appeared. Valid responses were counted from the onset of the stopwatch and up to 500 ms. Responses given after 500 ms and up to 30,000 ms were counted as a lapse. The administration lasted 10 min. Standard PVT outcomes were included in the analysis: reciprocal mean reaction time (1/MeanRT*1000(seconds)) (higher values indicate better performance), the total number of lapses (RT > 500 ms) (higher values indicate worse performance), and median RT (ms) (higher values indicate worse performance) (Basner and Dinges 2011 ; Lopez et al. 2012 ).

The DSST was administered to measure processing speed. The current version is an adapted version from Wechsler ( 1939 ). Participants were presented with nine symbols at the top of the computer screen. Each symbol matched a single number from 1 to 9. Below were blank boxes with one symbol above each box. The participants were given 120 s to type the number that corresponded to each symbol as fast as possible. Participants were not able to change their responses or go back once they hit a number. The number of correct symbols within the time limit constituted the score, with a higher score indicating a better performance.

The LOT was administered to measure visuospatial abilities and was originally designed by Benton et al. ( 1978 ). In the current version, participants were presented with 20 lines at a specific angle, one at a time, and had to identify the matching lines from a set of 15 line options below. The task took approximately 3 min to complete. These equally long lines were distributed equally over a 180° half‐circle. Participants were told to select, with their computer mouse, one of the 15 lines they believed had the same angle as the target line. A timer was located on the right side of the screen counting down the 10 s they had to respond to each line. Each trial was scored as correct or incorrect and scores ranged from 0 to 20, with 20 being a perfect score.

All participants took home a self‐applied polysomnography (PSG) device (Nox Medical, A1s, Reykjavik, Iceland) for three consecutive nights (Dimitri et al. 2024 ). The PSG included frontal electroencephalography (AF4, AF3, AF8, and AF7), electrooculography (E1, E2, E3, and E4), oximeter, electrocardiography, accelerometer, nasal cannula, thorax and abdomen respiratory inductance plethysmography belts, leg electromyography, and audio. For statistical analysis, average scores from the three consecutive nights were calculated. There were 17 participants that had one invalid night with an average taken from two nights, and eight participants that had two invalid nights with scores from one night. Scoring was performed in Noxturnal 6.2.2. software system (Nox Medical, Reykjavik, Iceland). The PSGs were manually scored by an expert sleep technologist following the guidelines from the AASM Manual for the Scoring of Sleep and Associated Events Version 2.6 (Berry et al. 2020 ). This included manual scoring on the AHI, arousal index (AI), oxygen desaturation index (ODI) < 3% (the number of oxygen desaturation events of ≥ 3 per hour of sleep) and hypoxia < 90% (time spent below 90% SpO 2 ). The following changes to the scoring deviating from the AASM manual were made based on a previous (Rusanen et al. 2023 ) publication comparing the traditional PSG and self‐applied PSG setup used in this study: low pass filter setting for EEG was changed from 0.3 to 0.5 Hz and the peak to peak amplitude of the slow wave activity was changed from 75 to 45 μV. Participants were grouped into OSA severity groups based on the AHI where no OSA is indicated by 0–4.9 events/h, mild OSA by 5–14.9 events/h, moderate by 15–29.9, and severe OSA by ≥ 30 events/h (AASM 1999 ).

The ABOSA signal analysis software was used to automatically calculate different SpO 2 parameters capturing hypoxic load (Karhu et al. 2022 ), including average SpO 2 during sleep and ODI < 4%. The desaturation and recovery event parameters included were (1) desaturation severity (DesSev) defined as the fall area (i.e., the sum of the areas of oxygen desaturation events starting from the onset of desaturation and ending to the nadir), (2) desaturation severity from 100% baseline (DesSev100) (i.e., the sum of the areas of oxygen desaturation events starting from 100% oxygen saturation baseline and ending to the nadir), and (3) desaturation duration (DesDur) defined as the fall duration (i.e., the sum of durations of the scored desaturation events). The same parameters were assessed for the recovery part of events (from the nadir to the offset of the desaturation) (Kulkas, Tiihonen, Julkunen, et al. 2013 ). For data analysis, desaturation and recovery events were combined to capture whole desaturation events from onset back to baseline: DesSev + RecSev = Hypoxic severity, DesSev100 + RecSev100 = Hypoxic severity from 100% baseline, and DesDur + RecDur = Hypoxic duration. Average oxygen saturation during wake was separately calculated in Python (Van Rossum and Drake 2009 ). It was calculated as the average SpO 2 during the total time spent awake before the first 30‐s sleep epoch and after the last 30‐s sleep epoch. The wake time was measured at 2.2 h on average for the whole sample (median = 1.8 h, range = 180 s to 4.5 h). Four participants had less than 10 min of wake time; their data was manually reviewed and not identified as unusual. To minimise the impact of motion artefacts and other signal noise, SpO 2 values above 100% and below 60% were excluded. In addition, 11 recordings with average SpO 2 values below 80% were removed for the same reason.

Participants received an introduction letter about the study and were informed of their right to withdraw at any time. They signed a digital consent form using their electronic ID before participation. Before the visit, they completed a background questionnaire covering demographics, self‐reported sleep patterns, sleepiness, and medication use. All questionnaires and the digital consent form were collected and managed online using REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture) (Harris et al. 2009 , 2019 ). Upon arrival at Reykjavik University, either at 10:00 am or 12:00 pm, the participants' height and weight were measured. Participants then performed an in‐laboratory digital neurocognitive battery including 13 tests that took approximately 1.5 h to complete (Jóhannsdóttir et al. 2021 ). All tests were administered in the same order for each participant. Five of these tests were included in the current study measuring cognitive abilities known to be affected in OSA: verbal memory, vigilance, processing speed, cognitive flexibility, and visuospatial abilities (Andreou et al. 2014 ; Bucks et al. 2017 ; Engleman and Joffe 1999 ; Jóhannsdóttir et al. 2021 ; Kainulainen et al. 2020 ; Seda et al. 2021 ; Vanek et al. 2020 ). Two participants completed the neurocognitive battery at once in the same room with one study coordinator present to answer questions. The two participants could not see each other as their desks were separated by portable office walls. Their screens were the same size, they wore noise cancelling headphones, and headphone volumes were standardised. Subsequently, participants were provided with self‐applied PSG for a three‐night sleep study. Finally, participants completed the PROMIS questionnaire on self‐reported cognitive function after the visit.

For data analysis, the Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS, version 28.0) was used, and two‐tailed p values < 0.05 were considered significant. Participants were categorised by age into four groups (19–39, 40–49, 50–59, and 60+ years) and by sex as male or female. Levels of education were grouped into (a) primary, high school, vocational/technical degree, (b) undergraduate degree (BS/BA), and (c) postgraduate degree (MS/MA/MBA/PhD). Body mass index (BMI) was calculated from the height and weight measurements, with a BMI of 18.5–24.9 kg/m 2 defined as healthy, 25.0–29.9 as overweight, and ≥ 30 as obese (Keys and BroŽek 1953 ). The participants were grouped into three OSA severity groups based on the AHI: no OSA (0–4.9 events/h), mild OSA (5–14.9 events/h), and moderate/severe (≥ 15). Differences between two groups were evaluated using an independent sample t ‐test with continuous variables and chi‐square test with categorical variables. Differences between three or more groups were evaluated using one‐way ANOVA followed by a Bonferroni post hoc test to test each pair of groups. Generalised linear models (GLM) were conducted to examine the correlation between each PSG parameter and cognitive outcome variables while adjusting for confounders: sex, age, education, and BMI. Each GLM included a cognitive outcome variable as the dependent variable, along with all confounders and a single PSG predictor. This method was most suitable for the current dataset, which contains non‐normally distributed dependent variables: number of lapses (3.1 skewness), reciprocal MRT (−1.7 skewness), and TOL total score (−2.4 skewness). All remaining dependent variables showed skewness levels within ±1.0. The assumptions of multicollinearity among predictors (< 0.7), independence of observations, and linearity of predictors were not violated. Spearman's rank correlation was used for evaluating the correlation between non‐normally distributed variables and the Pearson correlation for normally distributed variables. Non‐normally distributed PSG variables included all traditional parameters and hypoxic load parameters (skewness levels larger than ±1.0). Average SpO 2 during wake and sleep followed a normal distribution.

The study protocol was approved by the Icelandic National Ethics Committee (VSN‐21‐070) and the Icelandic Data Protection Authority.
sections.results:
The mean age of the 61 participants was 46.9 years (SD = 15.4), ranging from 19 to 79 years. Females were on average significantly younger than males (mean 45.4, SD = 14.5 vs. mean 48.6, SD = 16.4, p = 0.04) but did not differ from men in education or BMI (data not shown). Table 1 shows demographics according to OSA severity groups based on the AHI. BMI severity groups differed by OSA severity, where those with moderate/severe OSA were more likely to be obese. Most of the participants with mild, moderate, and severe OSA were men, who also had, on average, lower SpO 2 during sleep compared to females (males 92.6%, SD = 1.9, females 93.8%, SD = 1.8, p = 0.009). Moreover, OSA severity based on other traditional and hypoxic load parameters was significantly worse among men (data not shown). By contrast, men did not differ from females in average SpO 2 during wake (males 93.6% SD = 1.5, females 94.1% SD = 1.8, p = 0.29).

Demographics of the study population according to traditional OSA severity groups.

Abbreviations: BMI = body mass index, HS = high school, OSA = obstructive sleep apnea, PS = primary school, SD = standard deviation, VS = vocational school.

p < 0.01.

Table 2 presents significant correlations between the assessed PSG parameters. Average SpO 2 during both sleep and wake was negatively correlated with other OSA severity parameters.

Correlation between all PSG parameters and average SpO 2 values.

Abbreviations: AHI = apnea‐hypopnea index, AI = arousal index, avg. SpO 2 = average oxygen saturation, Hypoxic sev. = hypoxic severity, ODI = oxygen desaturation index.

Correlation is significant at the 0.01 level.

Correlation is significant at the 0.05 level.

Average scores on cognitive outcomes and BMI did not differ between males and females (data not shown). However, 70.5% of those considered healthy according to the BMI were females, 62% of those grouped overweight were males, and 52% of those grouped obese were females. Higher education was not correlated with better cognitive performance since the single significant difference was found in visuospatial ability where the undergraduate group performed better (76.5% accuracy) compared to the postgraduate group (61.5% accuracy) ( p = 0.009). Age groups differed in immediate recall, total recall, processing speed, and cognitive flexibility with older groups performing worse than younger groups (see Table 3 ). OSA severity groups, based on the AHI classification, differed in immediate recall and total recall where the moderate/severe OSA group performed worse than the no OSA group. Processing speed also differed between OSA groups; however, the mild OSA group performed worse on processing speed than the moderate/severe OSA group (see Table 3 ).

Average scores on the neurocognitive tests by age and OSA severity groups based on the AHI.

Note : Data are shown as mean (standard deviation, SD) and significant findings in bold. From post hoc test p < 0.05, # with the first group inside each column, *with the last group inside each column.

Abbreviations: AHI = apnea‐hypopnea index, AVLT = auditory verbal learning test, DSST = digit symbol substitution test, LOT = line orientation task, MRT = median reaction time, OSA = obstructive sleep apnea, PVT = psychomotor vigilance task, RT = reaction time, TOL = Tower of London.

Correlations between each PSG parameter (respiratory and oxygen‐related parameters) and cognitive outcome variables are presented in Table 4 . Significant findings from generalised linear models (GLM's) are also presented in Table 4 in bold and demonstrate correlations after adjusting for age, sex, education, and BMI.

Correlations between PSG parameters and cognitive outcome variables.

Note : Significant generalised linear models (GLM) are presented in bold.

Abbreviations: AHI = apnea‐hypopnea index, AI = arousal index, avg. SpO 2 = average oxygen saturation, Cog. = cognitive, ODI = oxygen desaturation index, RT = reaction time, MRT = mean reaction time.

Correlation is significant at the 0.01 level.

Correlation is significant at the 0.05 level.

Verbal memory was measured with the AVLT and variables used were immediate recall, total recall, and learning over trials. There was no significant predictor for learning over trials and age was the only predictor of total recall ( χ 2 = 15.4–26.5, p < 0.001). However, two sleep parameters, along with age, significantly predicted immediate recall. The first sleep parameter was average SpO 2 during sleep ( χ 2 (6) = 28.935, p < 0.001) where higher SpO 2 values ( β = 0.38, SE = 0.18, 95% CI = [0.03, 0.73], p = 0.03) and lower age ( β = −0.06, SE = 0.02, 95% CI = [−0.1, −0.02], p = 0.003) predicted greater immediate recall ability. The second model included hypoxia < 90% ( χ 2 (6) = 29.428, p < 0.001) where less time spent below 90% SpO 2 ( β = −0.03, SE = 0.02, 95% CI = [−0.07, −0.01], p = 0.03) and lower age ( β = −0.07, SE = 0.02, 95% CI = [−0.10, −0.04], p = < 0.001) predicted better outcomes. Based on the magnitude of the beta coefficient, average SpO 2 during sleep was the stronger PSG predictor of immediate recall.

Processing speed was measured with the DSST, and GLM results showed that four sleep parameters and age predicted processing speed. The first significant GLM included ODI < 4% ( χ 2 (6) = 16.854, p = 0.010) where less oxygen desaturation events < 4% per hour of sleep ( β = −0.71, SE = 0.34, 95% CI = [−1.4, −0.03], p = 0.04) and lower age ( β = −0.76, SE = 0.25, 95% CI = [−0.1.2, −0.28], p = 0.002) predicted better processing speed. The second model included hypoxic severity ( χ 2 (6) = 16.833, p = 0.010) where increased hypoxic severity ( β = −9.31, SE = 4.5, 95% CI = [−18.20, −0.41], p = 0.40) and lower age ( β = −0.82, SE = 0.24, 95% CI = [−1.29, −0.34], p < 0.001) predicted better outcomes. The third significant GLM included hypoxic severity from 100% baseline ( χ 2 (6) = 17.740, p = 0.007) where increased hypoxic severity from 100% baseline ( β = −5.72, SE = 2.51, 95% CI = [−10.63, −0.79], p = 0.023) and lower age ( β = −0.73, SE = 0.25, 95% CI = [−1.22, −0.25], p = 0.003) predicted better outcomes. The fourth included hypoxic duration ( χ 2 (6) = 17.101, p = 0.009) where less hypoxic duration ( β = −0.60, SE = 0.28, 95% CI = [−1.16, −0.05], p = 0.034) and lower age ( β = −0.73, SE = 0.25, 95% CI = [−1.22, −0.245], p = 0.003) predicted better outcomes. Based on beta coefficients and standard errors, hypoxic severity from 100% baseline was the strongest PSG predictor of processing speed.

Vigilance was measured with the PVT and outcome variables number of lapses, median RT, and Reciprocal MRT. No GLM's were significant when predicting the number of lapses; however, median RT was predicted by average SpO 2 during sleep, sex, and education ( χ 2 (6) = 16.780, p = 0.10). Higher average SpO 2 levels during sleep ( β = −15.49, SE = 4.6, 95% CI = [−0.24.51, −6.46], p < 0.001), males ( β = 0.38, SE = 0.18, 95% CI = [0.03, 0.73], p = 0.03), and lower the lowest education group ( β = 27.20, SE = 12.96, 95% CI = [1.80, 52.60], p = 0.036) predicted lower median RT's. For reciprocal MRT, six sleep parameters were significant predictors along with age and education. The first significant GLM included hypoxia < 90% ( χ 2 (6) = 14.059, p = 0.030) where less time spent below 90% SpO 2 ( β = −0.01, SE = 0.004, 95% CI = [−0.02, −0.003], p = 0.010), males ( β = 0.34, SE = 0.12, 95% CI = [0.10, 0.58], p = 0.006) and the lowest education group ( β = −0.32, SE = 0.14, 95% CI = [−0.59, −0.05], p = 0.020) predicted better outcomes. The second included hypoxic duration ( χ 2 (6) = 12.995, p = 0.043) where less hypoxic duration ( β = −0.01, SE = 0.005, 95% CI = [−0.02, −0.002], p = 0.020), males ( β = 0.36, SE = 0.13, 95% CI = [0.11, 0.62], p = 0.005) and the lowest education group ( β = −0.27, SE = 0.14, 95% CI = [−0.55, −0.003], p = 0.047) predicted better outcomes. The third included hypoxic severity from 100% baseline ( χ 2 (6) = 14.123, p = 0.028) where a decrease in hypoxic severity from 100% baseline ( β = −0.11, SE = 0.04, 95% CI = [−0.20, −0.03], p = 0.010), males ( β = 0.37, SE = 0.13, 95% CI = [0.12, 0.62], p = 0.004) and the lowest education group ( β = −0.28, SE = 0.14, 95% CI = [−0.55, −0.013], p = 0.040) predicted better outcomes. The fourth included average SpO 2 during sleep ( χ 2 (6) = 16.718, p = 0.010) where higher SpO 2 values during sleep ( β = 0.15, SE = 0.05, 95% CI = [0.06, 0.24], p = 0.002), males ( β = 0.42, SE = 0.13, 95% CI = [0.17, 0.67], p < 0.001), and the lowest education group ( β = −0.34, SE = 0.13, 95% CI = [−0.60, −0.08], p = 0.012) predicted better outcomes. The fifth included average SpO 2 during wake ( χ 2 (6) = 15.046, p = 0.020) where higher SpO 2 values during wake ( β = 0.11, SE = 0.04, 95% CI = [0.03, 0.19], p = 0.005), males ( β = 0.23, SE = 0.12, 95% CI = [0.003, 0.461], p = 0.048) and the lowest education group ( β = −0.29, SE = 0.14, 95% CI = [−0.57, −0.03], p = 0.032) predicted better outcomes. The last model included the arousal index ( χ 2 (6) = 12.666, p = 0.049) where an increased number of arousals per hour of sleep ( β = −0.02, SE = 0.01, 95% CI = [−0.03, −0.003], p = 0.02) and males ( β = 0.35, SE = 0.13, 95% CI = [0.09, 0.59], p = 0.007) predicted better outcomes. Based on the magnitude of the beta coefficients and standard errors, average SpO 2 during sleep was the strongest PSG predictor of vigilance performance that is, reciprocal MRT.

No sleep parameter predicted cognitive flexibility (TOL) or visuospatial abilities (LOT) (data not shown).
sections.discussion:
We found that hypoxic load parameters measuring OSA severity are stronger predictors of cognitive performance known to be affected in OSA, compared to more traditional parameters including the AHI. Results from generalised linear models (GLM), adjusted for age, sex, education, and BMI, supported our hypothesis as no correlations were found between the AHI and cognitive outcome variables. Additionally, the strongest PSG predictors of cognitive abilities were hypoxic severity from 100% baseline and average SpO 2 during sleep. Hypoxic severity from 100% baseline was the strongest PSG predictor of processing speed, and average SpO 2 during sleep was the strongest predictor of immediate recall and vigilance. Several other hypoxic parameters were significant predictors of cognitive abilities. Among the traditional parameters, hypoxia < 90% predicted immediate recall and vigilance, the AHI predicted vigilance, and ODI < 4% predicted processing speed. Regarding novel hypoxic load parameters, hypoxic severity predicted processing speed, and hypoxic severity from 100% baseline and hypoxic duration predicted processing speed and vigilance. Finally, average SpO 2 levels during sleep also predicted processing speed. No sleep parameter predicted cognitive flexibility or visuospatial abilities.

Our second hypothesis was that average SpO 2 during wake would be associated with cognitive performance independently of OSA severity. Our results demonstrated an association between both lower average SpO 2 levels during wake and sleep with worse vigilance performance. This raises important questions about underlying mechanisms driving oxygen saturation fluctuations during wake. Potential contributing factors could be underlying cardiovascular or pulmonary conditions (James et al. 2020 ; Voulgaris et al. 2021 ), or increased metabolic demand during wakefulness. However, the results should be interpreted with caution, as the timing of the wake SpO 2 measurement does not capture fluctuations throughout the full wake period. Nonetheless, the findings emphasise the need for further investigation into daytime oxygen saturation fluctuations and their potential impact on cognitive abilities.

The results align with the previous literature where the AHI is associated with cognitive performance; these include studies where the average age of participants is similar to those in the current study (Batool‐Anwar et al. 2014 ; Hrubos‐Strøm et al. 2012 ; Kainulainen et al. 2020 ; Quan et al. 2011 ; Thorisdottir et al. 2024 ). Regardless, a prior study including 2.090 men with a higher average age, 76 ± 6 years, also showed no association between the AHI and vigilance, cognitive flexibility, and global cognition (Blackwell et al. 2011 ) suggesting that the lack of associations between the AHI and cognitive abilities is not age dependent. The association between hypoxia < 90% and vigilance has also previously been found (avg. age 42.0) (SD = 12.7) (Alomri et al. 2021 ), including the association between hypoxic severity and vigilance (avg. age 56.8 46.4–66.7) (Kainulainen et al. 2020 ). The results further support previous findings where average SpO 2 during sleep, but not the AHI, was associated with verbal memory (Hrubos‐Strøm et al. 2012 ; Thorisdottir et al. 2024 ).

It has been well established that increased age is linked to reduced cognitive performance, for example, in memory, processing speed, and cognitive flexibility (Amelchenko et al. 2023 ; Dahan et al. 2020 ; Manard et al. 2014 ; Murman 2015 ; Zhao et al. 2021 ). The current findings are consistent with the literature where average scores on verbal memory, cognitive flexibility, and processing speed differed between age groups, with the youngest participants performing better than other age groups. Furthermore, GLM analyses showed that age remained a strong predictor of immediate recall and processing speed after accounting for the effects of other covariates. Higher education has been shown to be associated with better cognitive performance (Lövdén et al. 2020 ), and although differences in mean scores on the cognitive tests between education groups were not observed, GLM's showed a correlation between the lowest education group and vigilance (reciprocal MRT) after adjustment for confounders.

The study has a few limitations. The small sample size may limit the ability to capture true effects of OSA severity on cognitive abilities. The average age was relatively young or 46.9 years, reducing the likelihood of detecting cognitive difficulties that may develop over many years after disease onsetA control group for normative data on the cognitive tests would have been beneficial for baseline comparison, and the inability to include delayed recall in the analyses due to too short intervals was limiting. Potential confounders affecting cognitive performance, including prior night's sleep, sedatives, caffeine, and nicotine, were not controlled Wake SpO 2 measurements are also methodologically challenging due to sensitivity to posture, activity, and transitional states, and do not reflect fluctuations across the full wake period. The study's strength include the incorporation of various PSG parameters, both novel and traditional measures of respiration and oxygen‐related parameters. We consider the selection of cognitive tests to be a strength of the study since they have all been suggested to be used in sleep research (Jóhannsdóttir et al. 2021 ). We also consider the inclusion of average SpO 2 during wake a considerable strength and is to our knowledge is the first study to do so when evaluating cognitive performance in OSA. However, the calculation of average wake SpO 2 is limiting as it did not capture the whole wakefulness period and was calculated as the mean SpO 2 before the first non‐wake 30‐s epoch and after last non‐wake epoch, which varied in length across individuals.

In conclusion, the study showed that oxygen saturation‐based parameters are associated with cognitive performance and not the AHI. Hypoxic severity from 100% SpO 2 baseline best predicted processing speed, and average SpO 2 during sleep best predicted immediate recall and vigilance. The results underline the importance of understanding the relationship between cognitive function and SpO 2 ‐based OSA severity parameters. We propose longitudinal studies to examine potential late‐onset cognitive difficulties in OSA, to include larger clinical cohorts of OSA patients for larger effects, and for sleep research to include measures of SpO 2 during wake for a full picture of the relationship between oxygen saturation and cognitive measures in sleep research.
